title: What does OSHA require for crane operator certification and evaluation?
description: 29 CFR 1926.1427 after the 2018 rule: crane operator training, certification or licensing, the documented evaluation, and operator-in-training limits.
shortAnswer: Under 29 CFR 1926.1427, as revised by the Occupational Safety and Health Administration (OSHA) in November 2018, construction employers must ensure each crane operator is trained, certified or licensed, and evaluated before operating covered equipment. Certification by an accredited testing organization or an audited employer program is valid for 5 years. Separately, the employer must evaluate the operator's skills and ability to recognize and avert risk on the actual equipment, and document that evaluation.
keyTakeaways: The 2018 rule (83 FR 56244) made the section effective December 10, 2018, with the evaluation and documentation requirements effective February 7, 2019.

Operators must be licensed where a qualifying state or local license exists, and otherwise certified by an accredited crane operator testing organization or through an audited employer program, at no cost to the employee.
Accredited certifications are based on equipment type, or type and capacity, are portable among employers and are valid for 5 years. Audited employer certifications are not portable.

Certification does not make an operator qualified on its own: paragraph (f) requires an employer evaluation on the equipment, documented with the operator's name, evaluator's name and signature, date, and the equipment's make, model and configuration.
Derricks, sideboom cranes and equipment rated at 2,000 pounds or less are excepted from 1926.1427, though other training requirements still apply.
jurisdiction: United States (federal, with OSHA-approved State Plans)
regulator: Occupational Safety and Health Administration (OSHA), US Department of Labor
appliesTo: Construction employers whose employees operate cranes and other equipment covered by 29 CFR 1926 Subpart CC
Operator's trainers and evaluators acting as employees or agents of the employer
Crane operator testing organizations and auditors of employer certification programs

sections.heading: What must an employer ensure before someone operates a crane?

blocks.text: That the operator is trained, certified or licensed, and evaluated. Paragraph (a) of [29 CFR 1926.1427](https://www.law.cornell.edu/cfr/text/29/1926.1427) says "The employer must ensure that each operator is trained, certified/licensed, and evaluated in accordance with this section before operating any equipment covered under subpart CC." Until all three are met, the employee may only operate as an operator-in-training under paragraph (b).

The current text comes from a final rule published at 83 FR 56244 on November 9, 2018. Paragraph (k) makes the section effective December 10, 2018, except the evaluation and documentation requirements in paragraphs (a) and (f), which took effect on February 7, 2019. OSHA's [crane, derrick and hoist safety page](https://www.osha.gov/cranes-derricks) also records an earlier November 9, 2017 rule that set November 10, 2018 as the compliance date for operator certification.

Paragraph (a)(2) excepts operators of derricks, sideboom cranes and equipment with a maximum manufacturer-rated hoisting or lifting capacity of 2,000 pounds or less, but notes that the training requirements in those equipment sections continue to apply. Paragraph (a)(3) treats a current US military operator qualification as meeting the section for federal employees of the Department of Defense or Armed Forces, valid only with the issuing employer.

blocks.title: Currency
blocks.text: This page reflects 29 CFR 1926.1427 and 1926.1430 as at November 2026. Some states and cities run their own crane operator licensing, and paragraph (c)(1) requires operators to hold that license where it meets the federal criteria. State Plan states may also set additional requirements.

sections.heading: What are the routes to crane operator certification or licensing?

blocks.text: Licensing by a qualifying state or local government where one exists; otherwise certification by an accredited testing organization or through an audited employer program. The routes differ mainly in portability.

blocks.text: Paragraph (c)(3) requires the employer to provide certification or licensure "at no cost to employees." Under paragraph (e)(5), if an auditor finds a significant deficiency in an employer program, no operator may be qualified until it is corrected, the program must be re-audited within 180 days, and the auditor must report the deficiency to the OSHA Regional Office within 15 days.

A written test of equipment knowledge and a practical test of operating skill, both defined in paragraph (j). The written test must show the candidate knows the controls and operational characteristics, can use and calculate load and capacity information across configurations, knows procedures for preventing and responding to power line contact, has technical knowledge of the Appendix C criteria and of ground conditions and site hazards, and knows Subpart CC. It must also show the candidate can read and locate information in the equipment manual.

The practical test must show the ability to recognize the shift inspection items in 1926.1412(d) by sight and sound, operational and maneuvering skills, application of load chart information, and safe shut-down and securing procedures. Under paragraph (h), tests may be given verbally to a candidate who passes a written literacy demonstration, and in any language the candidate understands, but the operator may then only run equipment whose manuals and load charts are in the language of certification.

sections.heading: What is the employer evaluation, and how must it be documented?

blocks.text: It is the employer's own check that the operator can run the specific equipment safely for the assigned work, and it is separate from certification. Paragraph (f)(1) requires an evaluation demonstrating "the skills and knowledge, as well as the ability to recognize and avert risk, necessary to operate the equipment safely," including those specific to safety devices, operational aids, software, and size and configuration (lifting capacity, boom length, attachments, luffing jib and counterweight set-up), plus the ability to perform the hoisting activities required, such as blind lifts, personnel hoisting and multi-crane lifts.

Paragraph (f)(3) is the key change from earlier practice: "Possession of a certificate or degree cannot, by itself, cause a person to be qualified for purposes of paragraph (f)(1)." The evaluator must have the knowledge, training and experience to assess operators and must be an employee or agent of the employer. Once evaluated, the operator may run other equipment the employer can show does not require substantially different skills, knowledge or risk recognition.

Paragraph (f)(6) requires documentation with "the operator's name; the evaluator's name and signature; the date; and the make, model, and configuration of equipment used in the evaluation," available at the worksite while the operator is employed. For operators employed before December 10, 2018, paragraph (f)(2) allows the employer to rely on previous assessments, with documentation of the date of that determination and the equipment on which competency was shown. Paragraph (f)(7) requires re-evaluation on the subject of any retraining.

Operate within their ability under continuous monitoring by a trainer, but not in five high risk situations unless certified. Paragraph (b) requires a combination of formal and practical instruction, continuous on-site monitoring by an operator's trainer who performs no distracting tasks, and line of sight plus verbal or hand signal communication (direct communication for tower cranes). Trainer breaks are limited to 15 minutes and no more than one per hour, with tasks set in advance.

Under paragraph (b)(3), an operator-in-training must not operate where the equipment could get within 20 feet of a power line up to 350 kV or 50 feet of a line over 350 kV, when hoisting personnel, in multiple-equipment lifts, over a shaft, cofferdam or in a tank farm, or in multiple-lift rigging operations unless the trainer judges the trainee's skills sufficient. Paragraph (b)(5) requires retraining when performance or an evaluation indicates it is necessary.

sections.heading: How can a contractor evidence crane operator compliance?

blocks.text: Hold three linked records for each operator: certification or license, the paragraph (f) evaluation for each equipment configuration, and any retraining with its re-evaluation. The table below is an original, illustrative mapping. For the general approach to observed skill checks, see [verification of competency](/glossary/verification-of-competency) and [how to set up verification of competency](/guides/how-to-set-up-verification-of-competency).

blocks.text: Excepted equipment still needs training: 1926.1430(c)(2) requires the employer to train operators covered by the paragraph (a)(2) exception on the safe operation of the equipment they will use. For the general OSHA training framework, see [OSHA training requirements](/regulations/osha-training-requirements).

sections.heading: How does Knowledge Foundry approach this?

blocks.text: Knowledge Foundry structures crane operation as a framework of equipment types, configurations, hoisting activities and risks, and links the evaluation criteria in paragraph (f) to each. Evaluations and retraining can then be traced to the specific configuration and skill they cover, which is the level of detail the documentation rule requires.

faqs.q: Is a crane operator certification enough to operate any crane?
faqs.a: No. Certification shows the operator passed tests for an equipment type, or type and capacity. Paragraph (f)(3) states that a certificate cannot by itself make the operator qualified, and the employer must evaluate the operator on the equipment and configurations they will use and document that evaluation.

faqs.q: How long is crane operator certification valid?
faqs.a: Certifications from an accredited testing organization or an audited employer program are valid for 5 years. A state or local license is valid for the period the licensing office sets, but no longer than 5 years for compliance with 1926.1427. Military qualifications last as long as the issuing entity specifies.

faqs.q: Does a new employer have to re-evaluate an experienced operator?
faqs.a: Yes, for operators hired after December 10, 2018. The evaluation is the employer's own duty and must be documented on the equipment configuration used. An accredited certification is portable, but the evaluation is not. Employers may rely on earlier assessments only for operators they employed before December 10, 2018.

faqs.q: Who pays for crane operator certification?
faqs.a: The employer. Paragraph (c)(3) says that whenever certification or licensure is required under the section, the employer must provide it at no cost to employees.
